name: Scenario model and editor
type: Design decision (architecture): scenario data model, editor scope, storage/sharing and baseline-vs-proposal comparison
maintainer: Our project (synthesised from A/B Street by Dustin Carlino / A/B Street Ltd; Eclipse SUMO by DLR; traffic-simulation.de by Martin Treiber; PTV Vissim; Aimsun Next; Gaia3D-led Korean IITP project presented at FOSS4G 2025/2026; Streetmix)
first_release: N/A for our design. Reference points: A/B Street started 2018; Vissim/Aimsun scenario managers are long-standing commercial features; Korean platform first presented at FOSS4G 2025 (Nov 2025), third year presented at FOSS4G 2026 (Sep 2026).
last_activity: 2026-09-01 (FOSS4G 2026 talk 'Web-Based High-Performance Traffic Simulator', third project year); Aimsun Next 26.0.x docs on scenarios/experiments current in 2026
licence: Reference tools: A/B Street Apache-2.0; SUMO EPL-2.0 [uncertain: not re-verified in this pass]; traffic-simulation.de GPL-3.0; Vissim and Aimsun proprietary; Korean platform described as open source but licence not named [uncertain]
language: Our build: TypeScript (scenario schema as plain JSON). References: A/B Street Rust; traffic-simulation.de JavaScript; SUMO C++ with XML scenario files; Korean platform CesiumJS + OpenLayers + PostGIS
code_availability: References with public source: A/B Street (github.com/a-b-street/abstreet), traffic-simulation.de (github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de), SUMO (github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo). Korean platform: talks only, repository link not found [uncertain]. Vissim/Aimsun: proprietary binaries.
maintenance_health: A/B Street's original monolith slowed after a near-postmortem; the author split it into smaller tools and A/B Street Ltd now develops planning tools (README, 2025). Korean platform is grant-funded (IITP RS-2024-00459703), now in year 3. traffic-simulation.de is a single-author project with 550 commits. Implication: the scenario schema should not depend on any one upstream staying alive.
network_import: Patterns observed: (1) SUMO osmWebWizard pulls an OSM bounding box and writes osm_bbox.osm.xml, then builds osm.net.xml plus osm.poly.xml, osm.sumocfg and per-mode trips/routes into a timestamped folder; the network is a derived artefact, not the user-edited object. (2) A/B Street converts OSM into its own map model (slow, minutes) and then applies user edits incrementally on top, so edits must survive map regeneration from newer OSM. (3) The Korean platform takes Seoul/Daejeon network and station data as GeoJSON/PostGIS. Recommendation for our build: keep a versioned, immutable base network (hand-built preset or pre-converted OSM extract, identified by networkId + networkVersion) and store scenarios purely as edits keyed to stable link/node IDs, never as a copy of the network.
demand_input_formats: Observed: SUMO routes/trips XML per mode, generated by osmWebWizard from a 'Count' (vehicles per hour per lane-km) and a 'Through Traffic Factor' weighting boundary edges; Aimsun scenario references a Traffic Demand object made of OD matrices that can be scaled by a factor (tutorial duplicates demand at 120%); traffic-simulation.de exposes only Inflow, On-ramp Flow and Truck percentage sliders; Korean platform lets users configure different demand conditions before running. Minimal schema for us: demand = list of {originZoneOrEntryLink, destinationZoneOrExitLink, vehiclesPerHour, timeProfile (constant or piecewise 15-min multipliers)} + one global vehicle-mix object {car, twoWheeler, autoRickshaw, bus, truck, bicycle shares summing to 1} + globalDemandMultiplier (slider, e.g. 0.5-1.5) + randomSeed + durationMinutes + warmUpMinutes.
data_access: No dataset; the scenario file itself is the data artefact. Sharing without a backend: (a) JSON file export/import (A/B Street saves proposals locally as JSON); (b) URL fragment carrying compressed JSON of the edit list only (feasible because edits are small diffs against a known base network; base network itself must not be URL-encoded) [uncertain: practical URL length limits vary by browser and by the chat/social app where links are pasted]; (c) optional anonymous upload returning a share URL, as A/B Street did with a small Go API on Google App Engine storing files in Cloud Storage keyed by MD5 checksum for de-duplication. A/B Street notes the trade-off: anonymous uploads cannot be edited or deleted and authorship cannot be proven.
runs_in_browser_or_server: Scenario editor and storage: browser (localStorage/IndexedDB + file export + URL fragment). Engine: browser (leading option) or SUMO on a server; the schema should be engine-agnostic so either can consume it, matching the Korean platform's stated design of integrating with external simulation engines via import/export.
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: Schema is plain JSON, so it works with an in-browser TypeScript engine directly and can be transpiled to SUMO XML (net edits via netconvert/netedit-equivalent operations, closures as rerouter closingReroute/closingLaneReroute in an additional file, bus stops/parking as additional elements, demand as route/trip XML) for a server path. Results should be stored as compact aggregate time series per link/junction, not full trajectories, so that baseline and proposal results can both be held client-side for comparison.
api: Recommended internal API surface: loadBaseNetwork(networkId, version); applyEdits(network, edits[]) -> derivedNetwork (pure, deterministic, validates each edit); run(derivedNetwork, demand, seed, duration) -> ResultSet; compare(ResultSet baseline, ResultSet proposal) -> DeltaSet. This mirrors A/B Street's live-edit pipeline (diff edits vs current map, recompute only changed roads/intersections/turns, then refresh routing and drawing) and Vissim's base network + modifications + scenarios structure.
performance: A/B Street found full map conversion takes minutes, so it applies edits incrementally (diff, recompute affected turns/intersections, reuse node ordering for contraction hierarchies, defer full recompute until leaving edit mode). For a 72-hour build on a small network, full re-derivation on 'Run' is acceptable; incremental editing is a later optimisation. Running baseline and proposal with the same seed doubles compute per comparison [uncertain: no measured numbers for our engine yet].
gpu_requirement: None for the scenario model. Rendering may use WebGL/Canvas (the Korean platform uses CesiumJS 3D and OpenLayers WebGL 2D), but a 72-hour build should use 2D canvas only.
multi_tenancy_model: Client-side scenario state means zero per-user hosting cost for the editor; sharing via URL/JSON needs no server. If an anonymous share endpoint is added later, it is a write-once blob store (A/B Street pattern), which is cheap but cannot support edit/delete without accounts. The Korean platform instead uses a microservice architecture with PostGIS, which is heavier than a 72-hour budget allows.
build_complexity: Low-to-moderate if the edit vocabulary is kept small. A/B Street's retrospective warns that edits have knock-on effects (changing one road's lanes invalidates nearby signal policy; widening/narrowing roads at consolidated intersections creates hard geometry cases; undo/redo must handle these). Estimated 72-hour budget: schema + validation + JSON/URL import-export about 4-6 hours; editor panels for 6-8 edit types about 10-14 hours; comparison view about 6-8 hours [uncertain: estimate, not measured].
scenario_editability: What reference tools let users edit: A/B Street - lane types (driving, bus, bike, parking; sidewalks fixed), speed limits, lane direction reversal, stop-sign priority, traffic-signal timing, plus closing lanes/roads to force rerouting. SUMO - network via netedit, closures via rerouters (time-bounded), parking areas and bus stops as additional-file elements, demand via route files. traffic-simulation.de - only global sliders (inflow, on-ramp flow, truck %, v0, time gap T, max accel a, politeness, LC threshold, right bias) on fixed geometries. Korean platform - roads, routes, simulation parameters, demand; 2026 adds precise editing of overpasses/underpasses. Recommended minimal scenario schema (fields): scenarioId; name; description; author (optional); createdAt; schemaVersion; baseNetworkId; baseNetworkVersion; parentScenarioId (null for baseline; enables baseline -> proposal lineage); edits[] where each edit = {editId, type, targetId, params, enabled} and type is one of: setLinkLanes {laneCount}; setLinkWidth {carriagewayWidthM, effectiveWidthM}; setLinkSpeedLimit {kmh}; setLinkDirection {oneWay|twoWay}; closeLink {from, to times optional, allowedClasses optional}; setParking {side, lengthM or fractionOfLink, effectiveWidthLossM}; addBusStop {linkId, offsetM, bayOrKerbside, dwellSeconds, busesPerHour}; setSignalPlan {junctionId, cycleS, phases[{greenS, amberS, movements[]}], offsetS}; setJunctionControl {signal|priority|uncontrolled|roundabout}; setTurnBan {fromLink, toLink}; setGradeSeparation {flyoverLinkId, enabled, rampLinks[]} (toggle a pre-drawn flyover rather than free-form 3D editing); demand {as in demand_input_formats}; sim {seed, durationMin, warmUpMin, stepS}; indianBehaviour {seepageEnabled, laneDisciplineFactor} as named presets rather than raw parameters. Each edit must be independently toggleable so a proposal can be bisected.
output_metrics_supported: Views planners found useful in references: A/B Street trip-summary tab comparing trip times before vs after edits in aggregate with filters, side-by-side A/B runs, delay scatter plot, trip table; Korean platform side-by-side comparison view, time filter, route-change analyser, trip-line animation, OD matrix with flow arrows, congestion heatmaps, time-series layers with playback, dashboard reports; traffic-simulation.de virtual detector and trajectory export; Aimsun replications with distinct random seeds to show run-to-run variability. The IISc review of the 2026 Hebbal microsimulation report shows the failure to avoid: different metrics were reported for different scenarios, making comparison 'difficult, erroneous' and recommendations questionable. Recommended fixed metric set reported identically for every scenario: network-wide average travel time and delay per vehicle (by vehicle class); throughput (vehicles exiting per hour); max and average queue length per approach; link speed/density map coloured by level of service; per-junction delay table; vehicles still in network at end (unserved demand) and any gridlock/teleport count; delta view (proposal minus baseline) as a diverging-colour link map plus a summary table with absolute and percentage differences; result over multiple seeds (e.g. 3-5) shown as a range.
emissions_support: Not in the minimal scenario model. Could later add a derived CO2/fuel estimate per class; SUMO offers HBEFA-based emission models if the server path is used [uncertain: not verified in this pass].
known_limitations: (1) URL-encoded state only works when the base network is fixed and versioned; if the base network changes, old edit lists may point to missing IDs (A/B Street had to make edits survive map regeneration). (2) Anonymous share links cannot be edited, deleted or attributed (A/B Street). (3) Edits interact: lane changes invalidate signal plans and junction geometry (A/B Street retrospective). (4) Slider-only tools (traffic-simulation.de) are easy to use but cannot express network proposals; free-form editors (netedit, Vissim) are too complex for lay users. (5) Vissim propagates base-network edits into all scenarios and some scenario-management actions cannot be undone, so PTV advises not editing the base network once scenarios exist. (6) A single stochastic run can mislead; Aimsun builds replications with distinct seeds for this reason. (7) Korean platform abstracts do not describe a scenario storage schema or comparison metrics in detail, so its design can only be inferred from talk abstracts.
documented_failures: A/B Street: the author calls the scope 'way too broad' and describes an identity crisis between a game and a planning tool; the results 'have to be met with much more skepticism' because the model was not calibrated, and critics used that to dismiss it; edits needed complex handling for undo/redo side effects. Hebbal (Bengaluru) 2026 microsimulation report, per IISc technical review: promised four scenarios but analysed two; reported different metrics for different scenarios; claimed no spill-over without supporting data; network-level analysis limited to one link. Vissim: scenario-management operations cannot be undone and some commands become unavailable once a scenario's simulation starts.
validation_approach: For the editor/schema (not traffic realism): round-trip tests (export JSON -> import -> identical edit list; encode URL -> decode -> identical); schema-version migration test; each edit type validated against the base network (target exists, lane count >= 1, width >= lane count x minimum lane width, signal phases cover all movements); determinism test (same scenario + same seed -> identical results), which is a precondition for baseline-vs-proposal deltas to be meaningful; a no-op proposal (all edits disabled) must give zero delta.
takeaway_for_our_build: Adopt a Vissim/A/B-Street-style 'base network + ordered, toggleable edit list' model: baseline = base network + demand with zero edits; a proposal = the same plus edits, linked by parentScenarioId. Never let users edit the base network in the UI. Keep the edit vocabulary to about 8 types relevant to Indian streets (lanes, carriageway width, closures, on-street parking width loss, bus stops, signal plan, turn bans, toggle a pre-drawn flyover) plus demand multiplier and vehicle mix. Store everything as versioned JSON (schemaVersion, baseNetworkId, baseNetworkVersion); share by URL fragment (compressed edit list) and by JSON download/upload, with no backend in the 72-hour scope. Run baseline and proposal with identical seeds (ideally 3-5 seeds) and present one fixed metric set for every scenario, with a delta map and an absolute + percentage table; always show unserved demand and gridlock counts so a proposal cannot look good by hiding stuck vehicles. Follow the Korean workflow labels in the UI (Edit -> Simulate -> Visualize -> Compare) and copy its time filter. UX mistakes to avoid: exposing raw model parameters (use named presets), free-form 3D/grade-separation drawing, allowing edits during a run, silently resetting results after an edit (mark results stale instead), and reporting only percentages without absolute values (the IISc review shows small absolute gains looking large as percentages).
